你.etymology: The second-person pronoun is documented in the MOE dictionary with a quotation from Zhou Shu. This is evidence of earlier use, not a claim that the pronoun was first coined in that work.

history.stage: Zhou Shu, as quoted by MOE

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 你 (public-data mirror via 萌典)
Official MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 你

怎么.etymology: Written怎麼 in the traditional form, this question word covers why, how and in what way. The dictionary cites its use in Rulin Waishi and Honglou Meng; the lesson selects the reason-question meaning.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 怎麼 (public-data mirror via 萌典)
Official MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 怎麼

早.etymology: A single word serves for the morning, an early time and doing something earlier than expected. In this lesson early modifies arriving. The dictionary's range of meanings is useful history of usage, but does not date the first use of each sense.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 早 (public-data mirror via 萌典)
Official MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 早

到.etymology: The dictionary records reaching or arriving and cites that sense in Jiang Yan's Hen Fu. The modern arrival use is not an inflection: the same written word follows different people.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 到 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

了.etymology: The completion particle is read le, while another reading liǎo has senses including understand and finish. The MOE entry illustrates completed-actionle with Su Shi's Nian Nujiao. The two readings must not be treated as interchangeable in this dialogue.

history.stage: Su Shi, Nian Nujiao, as quoted by MOE

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 了 (public-data mirror via 萌典)
Official MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 了

我.etymology: The first-person pronoun is attested in the dictionary's quotations from the Yijing and Shijing. Its modern use for both I and me is a fact about sentence function, not a missing English-style case ending. No reconstructed ancient pronunciation is supplied here.

history.stage: Yijing and Shijing, as quoted by MOE

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 我 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

不.etymology: This is a long-established negative word. The dictionary distinguishes its usual bù reading from other literary readings. In ordinary Mandarin its tone can change before another fourth tone; that spoken adjustment does not make a new lemma.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 不 (public-data mirror via 萌典)
Official MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 不

像.etymology: The dictionary records appearance, an image and resembling something. Resemblance is illustrated with a quotation from Wang Chong's Lunheng. The lesson uses the comparison meaning; no story about the character's graphic origin is inferred from the modern components.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 像 (public-data mirror via 萌典)
Official MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 像

那么.etymology: Traditional那麼 is a fixed expression for a degree, manner or a link with what came before. The dictionary cites a conversational use in Ernu Yingxiong Zhuan. Here it sets the degree in a comparison rather than introducing a new consequence.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 那麼 (public-data mirror via 萌典)
Official MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 那麼

受.etymology: The receiving sense is documented alongside enduring and accommodating. A Li Bai quotation illustrates receiving an order. In受重用 the person receives important responsibilities; it is not a special passive suffix attached to the person's name.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 受 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

重用.etymology: The modern formation concerns valuing somebody highly and entrusting them with important work. The dictionary records this sense with quotations from Sanguo Yanyi and Wenming Xiaoshi. These are usage attestations, rather than a dated first coinage.

history.stage: Sanguo Yanyi, as quoted by MOE

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 重用 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

他们.etymology: Traditional他們 combines the third-person pronoun with the human plural marker們. The whole expression means they or them. This is a productive modern word formation, not evidence of gender or case endings on a Chinese verb.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 他們 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

没.etymology: The written word has distinct readings:méi for absence or negation and mò for sinking or being submerged. The dictionary cites the absence sense in a Wei Zhuang lyric. This source does not establish a chronological derivation of the negative from sinking.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 沒 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

给.etymology: Traditional給 has gěi for giving and jǐ in words concerning supply or provision. The lesson uses the ordinary act of giving someone work. These dictionary readings explain why guessing pronunciation from the isolated character is unsafe.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 給 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

多少.etymology: This combines the words for much and little into an expression for quantity. The dictionary records an amount asked about and a large or indefinite amount, with literary examples. Under the negative in the lesson it means they did not give her much work.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 多少 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

活.etymology: The dictionary records living or lively meanings and, separately, work or tasks. This scene uses the work sense. A learner should not translate the phrase as giving somebody many living things; the modern noun use is the relevant dictionary evidence.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 活 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

干.etymology: The simplified spelling干 represents幹 in the doing-work sense used here. The dictionary also records structural-support and main-body senses under幹. Their presence in one entry is not proof that any one sense directly caused the others; this lesson only needs gàn, do or work.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 幹 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

待.etymology: The dictionary separates dāi, stay, from dài, wait for or treat someone. The stay reading is illustrated in Ernu Yingxiong Zhuan. That reading distinction matters in the sentence about remaining for half a day.

history.stage: Ernu Yingxiong Zhuan, as quoted by MOE

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 待 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

半天.etymology: The components are half and day. The dictionary records both a literal half-day and a looser long while, illustrating the latter with Honglou Meng. The expression itself does not prove that a stay was measured to an exact number of hours.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 半天 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

就.etymology: The dictionary gives several functions, including taking up an activity and linking a following result. The lesson uses the short connective sense in an account of coming back. No single English word or ancient-origin story covers all its functions.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 就 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

回来.etymology: Traditional回來 combines returning with movement toward the present viewpoint. The dictionary's return-to-the-original-place meaning is illustrated in Rulin Waishi. The directional element distinguishes coming back from going back to somewhere else.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 回來 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

呗.etymology: Traditional唄 has a neutral conversational particle reading bei and a separate Buddhist chanting reading bài. The MOE entry lists both. Their shared written form does not establish that the casual sentence-ending particle was borrowed from Buddhist chanting.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 唄 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

那.etymology: The ordinary nà form can point to something farther away or connect with what was just said. The dictionary lists both uses and also other readings. The lesson's then or in-that-case function is not a question-word reading nǎ.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 那 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

先.etymology: The dictionary records preceding, earlier or first, as well as older nominal senses such as ancestors. Here it puts going inside before the other possible actions. No historical priority among those dictionary senses is claimed.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 先 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

进去.etymology: Traditional進去 combines entering with the directional wordgo. The dictionary defines movement from outside to inside. This modern directional structure explains the lesson without pretending there is a separate inflection for entering by one or two people.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 進去 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

啊.etymology: The dictionary distinguishes interjection readings from the light sentence-ending a. The latter adds conversational force rather than a new event. Its spelling alone cannot prescribe one fixed emotion or one English translation.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 啊 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

老师.etymology: Traditional老師 is a respectful word for a teacher. The dictionary also records an imperial-examination use in which a successful candidate addressed the chief examiner as teacher. Its present respectful force does not assert that every teacher is elderly.

history.meaning: respectful address to a chief examiner

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 老師 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

让.etymology: Traditional讓 has documented senses involving yielding, allowing and causing or asking someone to act. The lesson selects the request-to-wait meaning. The dictionary's older examples for other senses do not date the emergence of this particular conversational construction.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 讓 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

等.etymology: Alongside class or rank meanings, the dictionary records waiting. The lesson uses waiting for a person, placed directly after the word. Similar spelling across those meanings is not a reason to import the rank meaning into this exchange.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 等 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

一起.etymology: The dictionary records the established whole-word meaning together, illustrated in Wenming Xiaoshi, as well as a group or batch sense. These are documented uses of the compound. The consulted entry does not establish its earliest formation date.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 一起 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

免得.etymology: The dictionary defines this as avoiding an undesirable result and cites Shuihu Zhuan and Rulin Waishi. The lesson's explanation for waiting has exactly that preventive function. The second written component does not mean obtain independently in this fixed connective.

history.stage: Shuihu Zhuan, as quoted by MOE

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 免得 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

耽误.etymology: Traditional耽誤 names delay that causes something to go wrong. The dictionary records it with a quotation in Jin Shi. Its use for wasting somebody's time is broader than causing a typographical error, even though誤 also occurs in error vocabulary.

history.stage: Jin Shi, as quoted by MOE

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 耽誤 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

他.etymology: The dictionary records both a third-person pronoun and the older general senseother. The modern pronoun is illustrated in literary examples. The lesson identifies the male professor in writing; no reconstructed history of gendered pronoun spelling is asserted.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 他 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

的.etymology: The light grammatical readingde links an owner or description to what follows. The dictionary distinguishes this from other readings and meanings, including a target or certainty. Those other meanings are not literal translations of the possessive link in this lesson.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 的 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

时间.etymology: Traditional時間 is an established expression for duration or time. The dictionary also documents an older literary sense of the present moment. The lesson uses the broad time meaning, and the written components should not be mistaken for a modern scientific definition of time.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 時間 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

说.etymology: Traditional說 has distinct readings and senses: shuō for speaking or explaining, shuì for persuading and yuè in some older joyful expressions. The dictionary documents those differences. The ordinary speaking reading is the one used in this conversational invitation to consider the girl.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 說 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

这.etymology: Traditional這 is the near demonstrative contrasted with那. The dictionary records its use in Rulin Waishi and distinguishes a colloquial fused reading zhèi. The lesson uses the ordinary written form for this person.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 這 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

姑娘.etymology: The neutral-final-syllable expression for a young woman is distinguished from a fully toned regional kinship use for an aunt. The dictionary illustrates the young-woman use in Guanchang Xianxing Ji. The context and reading prevent a mistaken family relationship here.

history.stage: Guanchang Xianxing Ji, as quoted by MOE
history.meaning: a young woman, with neutral final syllable

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 姑娘 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

一点.etymology: Traditional一點 literally joins one with a point or small amount. The dictionary documents smallness and slight quantity. In the lesson the following negative makes the whole expression mean not the slightest bit; that is a constructional use, not a new plural form.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 一點 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

都.etymology: The dictionary separates dōu, all or even, from dū, a capital or major city. The lesson uses the inclusive or strengthening word. The capital-city meaning supplies no useful translation in either the two-student statement or the emphatic negative.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 都 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

刻薄.etymology: The dictionary records harsh or unkind treatment with a citation from Su Shi, and mocking somebody with a Honglou Meng example. In this scene the complete denial of such harshness is a playful compliment.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 刻薄 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

呢.etymology: The neutral particle ne has questioning and emphatic functions, illustrated in Ernu Yingxiong Zhuan and Lao Can Youji. The cloth reading ní is a different dictionary use. The question ending in this scene does not name a fabric.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 呢 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

走.etymology: Earlier examples recorded by the dictionary use走 for rapid movement or running, including the distinction in Shi Ming. The modern entry also includes walking and leaving. This makes the short invitation to get going understandable without forcing every use to mean run.

history.stage: Shi Ming, as quoted by MOE

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 走 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

吧.etymology: The neutral sentence ending ba is documented for suggestions, requests and related conversational uses. The dictionary separately lists bā in the transliterated word for a bar. The friendly suggestion in this lesson should not inherit that borrowing's etymology.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 吧 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

来.etymology: Traditional來 is the ordinary movement-toward-the-speaker word, illustrated by the dictionary's Analects quotation about friends coming from afar. That is a usage attestation, not an account of the ancient graph's shape. Repetition here welcomes the students closer.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 來 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

你们.etymology: Traditional你們 combinesyou with the human plural marker們. The dictionary cites the plural address in Rulin Waishi and Wenming Xiaoshi. It addresses more than one person; this lesson does not give it a polite singular function by analogy with French.

history.stage: Rulin Waishi, as quoted by MOE

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 你們 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

俩.etymology: Traditional倆 has liǎ for two people, distinguished from another reading in unrelated vocabulary. The dictionary illustrates liǎ with two sisters in Lao Can Youji. In the lesson it explicitly counts the two students; no following classifier is needed.

history.stage: Lao Can Youji, as quoted by MOE

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 倆 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

论文.etymology: Traditional論文 combines discussion with writing and is now an academic paper or thesis. The dictionary also cites the older literary-discourse use in Cao Pi's Dian Lun Lun Wen. That older work is not evidence that the modern university thesis system already existed in the same form.

history.stage: Cao Pi, Dian Lun Lun Wen, as quoted by MOE
history.meaning: literary discourse, distinguished from a modern thesis

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 論文 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

初稿.etymology: 初 supplies the initial stage and稿 a written draft. The dictionary contrasts this with a finalized version and cites Qing Bai Lei Chao. It describes the state of a document, not a verb tense that every written action must take.

history.stage: Qing Bai Lei Chao, as quoted by MOE

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 初稿 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

已经.etymology: Traditional已經 is an established already expression. The dictionary illustrates an action completed before the reference time in Rulin Waishi and Honglou Meng. The second graph is not translated as a physical thread or scripture in this whole-word temporal use.

history.stage: Rulin Waishi, as quoted by MOE

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 已經 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

通过.etymology: Traditional通過 has a documented passage-through sense, including a Song Shi citation, and an approval sense. The lesson uses passing review. This record distinguishes the senses without claiming that the approval sense began on the date of the cited passage-through example.

history.stage: Song Shi, as quoted by MOE

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 通過 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

接下来.etymology: This is a modern continuation expression built from接 and下來. The consulted dictionary records receiving or joining for接 and onward or following uses for下來. There is no exact whole-expression entry in the dataset reviewed, so its first historical attestation remains unestablished here.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 接 (public-data mirror via 萌典)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 下來 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

抓紧.etymology: Traditional抓緊 literally concerns gripping or holding firmly. The dictionary records that physical structure. With時間 in this scene it is a figurative instruction to make good use of time, not to clutch a physical clock.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 抓緊 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

把.etymology: The dictionary cites Shuowen for a grasping or holding sense and also records grammatical uses. Here把 sets up the affected object before the action. These sources do not by themselves date the entire development from a lexical verb to that grammatical construction.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 把 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

最终.etymology: Traditional最終 combines the extreme or utmost with the end. The dictionary defines the whole word as final or last. The transparent modern formation does not establish a particular ancient coinage date.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 最終 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

稿.etymology: The dictionary records both plant-stalk or straw meanings and a written or drawn draft. The written-draft sense is the relevant one in初稿 and最终稿. The consulted entry does not give the chronology connecting these senses.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 稿 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

交.etymology: The dictionary cites Shuowen's explanation involving crossed legs and records further interaction and transfer senses. The lesson uses handing something over. The old graphic explanation must not replace the modern submit meaning in this context.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 交 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

上来.etymology: Traditional上來 is a directional expression for movement upward or toward the current place, documented with a Honglou Meng example. After hand in, it orients the submission toward its receiver. It does not require the students to climb upstairs.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 上來 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

做.etymology: The dictionary records doing or carrying out a matter among the uses of做. Here the activity is making preparations. The same written form serves different people and times; the consulted entry does not establish the earliest date of this spelling.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 做 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

好.etymology: The dictionary distinguishes hǎo for good or satisfactory from hào for liking. After做 in this lesson it concerns bringing the preparation to a satisfactory result. The source supports this usage distinction without supplying a reconstructed graph history.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 好 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

答辩.etymology: Traditional答辯 concerns answering criticism or objections in the dictionary. In the university setting it is a thesis defence; official education sources document that academic use. The broader answering-and-defending structure is real, while the first date of its academic specialization is not established here.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 答辯 (public-data mirror via 萌典)
PRC Ministry of Education: use of 论文答辩 in graduate degree procedures

准备.etymology: Traditional準備 is documented as arranging or planning in advance, with a citation from Sanguo Yanyi. In the lesson it names the preparation the students must make. The word can also function as an action; this is not an inflected noun-versus-verb pair.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 準備 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

是.etymology: The dictionary records correctness, affirmation and identifying uses. The one-word reply here affirms that the professor’s instructions are accepted. These functions are documented under the same unchanged written form.

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 是 (public-data mirror via 萌典)

再见.etymology: Traditional再見 joins again and see or meet. The dictionary cites literal meeting again in Kongzi Jiayu and separately explains the current leave-taking formula. Those are distinct usage facts; the citation is not presented as the first recorded goodbye formula.

history.stage: Kongzi Jiayu, as quoted by MOE
history.meaning: literal meeting again, distinguished from the goodbye formula

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary: 再見 (public-data mirror via 萌典)
